stories.title: Man who killed 3 had schizophrenia relapse, court told
stories.summary: A 32-year-old man who killed three members of his family, stabbing them multiple times at their home in Co Louth last year, was suffering from a relapse of his schizophrenia at the time, the Central Criminal Court has heard. The court heard that experts on behalf of the defence and the prosecution agree that Robert O'Connor, from Drumgowna in Co Louth, had a mental disorder which substantially diminished his responsibility for the killings of his mother, father and younger brother in September 2025 and would allow the jury to find him guilty of manslaughter. However the psychiatric experts disagree about whether he qualifies for a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. Mr O'Connor pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to the murders of his father Mark, mother Louise, and younger brother Evan at their home between 28 and 29 September 2025, or alternatively, he pleaded guilty to manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility. Senior Counsel, Roisin Lacey for the prosecution began her opening speech to the jury last week. The remainder of the speech was postponed until today. Ms Lacey told the jurors that a couple of things required to be clarified and those clarifications had now come in.

stories.title: Govt accused of 'brinkmanship' over public sector strike
stories.summary: The Dáil has heard accusations the Government is engaging in a "game of brinkmanship...and chicken" with trade unions on the eve of a nationwide strike by over 300,000 public sector workers. Speaking in the Dáil during Leaders' Questions, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald called on the Taoiseach Micheál Martin "to intervene constructively" in the dispute and to pick up the phone and invite unions to talks, where pay is the "first item on the agenda". "You've known since June that a new pay deal had to be struck with the public sector workers. We find ourselves almost four months on, at the eleventh hour, on the brink of this strike action tomorrow. The reason we are here is because of a failure of your Government to engage and agree to enter into those talks processes in good faith," she said. "Why on earth are you engaging in this game of brinkmanship? Why on earth are you playing a game of chicken with public sector workers at a time when what we need is leadership," added the Dublin Central TD. "We've had ongoing contact with trade unions. We offered enhanced social dialogue earlier this year to the trade union movement," he said. "What I would say to you is we are open for discussion, we've invited in the unions for talks, and the Minister for Public Expenditure has said every issue they've raised is on the table," Mr Martin said.

stories.title: Dublin to host major AI summit amid safety concerns
stories.summary: Around 1,500 people are expected to attend a major international artificial intelligence (AI) summit at the RDS in Dublin. The event is expected to be one of the largest gatherings of the AI sector and policymakers in Europe this year, with Ireland hosting it as part of the country's EU presidency. The summit will look at research and innovation in AI, as well as issues around safeguards and security in the sector. Taoiseach Micheál Martin will give the opening address, with a number of industry speakers - including Microsoft's Vice Chair and President Brad Smith, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, and Anthropic's EMEA head Guillaume Princen - also taking to the main stage. The summit takes place against the backdrop of rising concern over appropriate safeguarding around AI, as the sector continues to grow at an exceptional rate. In recent months there have been numerous high-profile incidents where AI agents went rogue and hacked into government bodies and companies across the world.

stories.title: Democrats condemn federal search of Ilhan Omar home
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has been accused of "abusing his power" after the Washington home of Democrat Ilhan Omar was searched by US federal agents. A search was carried out at Ms Omar's home as part of what officials said was a criminal investigation, marking a dramatic escalation in Mr Trump's confrontation with the outspoken politician. Minnesota's Democratic Governor Tim Walz accused Mr Trump of "abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election." Ms Omar said she was "ok" following the operation, but accused the administration of targeting political opponents just three weeks before she seeks re-election in the 3 November midterms. The early morning search - described by Mr Trump's 'border czar' Tom Homan as part of a longstanding probe - was conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Ms Omar wrote on X.

stories.title: O'Sullivan pumped up for winter play-off bonanza
stories.summary: Denise O'Sullivan could potentially play five play-off matches in the space of a month for club and country as she looks to end a challenging 2026 in spectacular style. O'Sullivan left Liverpool last summer after less six months on Merseyside. Having spent so long in America, where she'd shone for North Carolina Courage in the NWSL, the Cork woman admits she just couldn't settle in England. Last July she made the call to move on, joining New York-based Gotham FC, who booked their place in the NWSL play-offs a few weeks ago with a 2-1 win over the Courage. The quarter-finals, semis and final all take place in November. O'Sullivan then goes straight into a blockbuster two-legged World Cup play-off final with the Republic of Ireland against Poland. The 32-year-old, who has had to contend with a knee injury in recent months, was rested for the first-leg semi-final hammering of Kazakhstan in Astana but she returned to the fray at SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh last night, scoring in a 4-0 win. "I'm excited to be honest," said O'Sullivan. "I think it's a challenge, and I think they're games that you want to be playing in. I mean, we're two games away from going to Brazil. It's an unbelievable to be in this position.

stories.title: Eight counties represented in Champion 15 hurling team
stories.summary: An eight-county spread of players who featured in the Christy Ring, Nickey Rackard and Lory Meagher Cup competitions makes up the 2026 Champion 15 hurling team of the year. Christy Ring Cup champions Derry are represented by goalkeeper Seán Kelly, defenders Patrick Turner and Conor Coyle, midfield engine Cormac O'Doherty and forwards Deaglán Foley and Shea Cassidy. New York’s second straight piece of silverware after adding the Nickey Rackard to the Meagher Cup won in 2025 is recognised with spots for the rampaging forward AJ Willis and defender and former Tipp footballer Bill Maher. Meanwhile 2026 Lory Meagher Cup winning captain Reuben Murray represents Longford alongside full-back colleague Seán Lancaster. Prolific Kerry forward Padraig Boyle is full-forward, while Sligo’s Andrew Kilcullen and Mayo’s Cormac Philips are other forwards who have had their lasting impact reflected on the team. Joe Murray’s defiance in defence for Leitrim earns him a place in the full-back line and Tyrone’s stylish Fionn Devlin completes the half-back line. The Champion 15 team, who will be honoured at Croke Park on Friday evening, was selected by an independent panel of Gaelic Games correspondents with nominations submitted by GPA player representatives.

stories.summary: Carla Ward has stayed true to her word by starting Katie McCabe and Denise O'Sullivan against Kazakhstan at SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh tonight, with Crystal Palace pair Hayley Nolan and Shanade Hopcroft also getting the nod. However Ward has urged her side to keep their foot on the gas as they look to end the window with another win and more goals. Captain McCabe was suspended for Friday's clash, while O'Sullivan was rested. They will offer even more firepower against the world's No 98-ranked team. Midfielder Hopcropt made her debut off the bench four days ago, scoring soon after her introduction. She goes into the engine room to make her first start beside hometown favourites O'Sullivan and Megan Connolly. Nolan slots into the central back three with Anna Patten and Jessie Stapleton, while Abbie Larkin will dovetail with Emily Murphy in attack.

stories.title: Issues remain up front as Ulster strive for consistency
stories.summary: Interprovincial matches are always tightly contested and Saturday's meeting between Munster and Ulster was no exception. Despite Munster racing into a commanding lead, the game finished on a knife-edge, with both sides trying to clinch the all-important winning score. Ulster have endured an awkward start to the season. A high-scoring draw away against Glasgow should be seen as a very respectable result. In their other two fixtures they chased down sizable deficits to draw with Munster and come within a score of a comeback win against Edinburgh. It is hardly the start Richie Murphy would have wanted as the province look to re-establish themselves in the top eight of the United Rugby Championship and secure their place among Europe’s elite. It’s also not the start to a match that the head coach of any team would want. Murphy spoke afterwards about their aim to start fast but Ulster let themselves down in the first 40 in Belfast. They have no problem scoring points in the second half of matches. It was a simple equation for Murphy, focus on the start and the rest will look after itself. That was not to be as Munster destroyed the hosts' setpiece and forced many errors in the Ulster attack. Kieran Brookes has been a surprise package for the Munster scrum. Aided by player of the match, Marnus Van Der Merwe, the visitors turned over an Ulster scrum against the feed to assert their scrum dominance over the northern province in the early stages of the game.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Ezra Williams' cultural picks
stories.summary: Ezra Williams is a Cork-based songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and producer. Their debut album Supernumeraries was nominated for the RTE Choice Music Prize, while their single My Own Person featured in Netflix drama Heartstopper. Catchy but subtle; self-deprecating but never sombre (and always utterly charming) their songs offer an often overlooked take on emotional relationships, with Ezra writing as a person who is non-binary and on the autism spectrum. They are currently working on new music for their next album. Ahead of their appearance at this year's Cork Jazz Festival, we asked Ezra for their choice cultural picks... I love the film Magnolia mainly for the soundtrack by Aimee Mann and I also love the movie Benjamin by Simon Amstell, again because of the soundtrack but also they’re both just very good movies. I usually rewatch films that have a good soundtrack, and I watch most films at home because I like being in bed when I watch a movie. Ive recently been listening to a lot of Lisa O’Neill, Remi Wolf, Stevie Wonder and Frog. Growing up, my main inspirations were Daniel Johnston, Elliott Smith and Kate Bush. In terms of genres, I listen to everything but recently I’ve been leaning more towards folk/trad music and country gaze. I try to go to as many gigs as possible. I don’t read books that much because of my dyslexia, so most of the books that I own are pattern books for knitting - I’m trying to teach myself lace patterns using a 280 Japanese lace stitches book. I’ve tried listening to audio books before, but I can never focus on them, I find it difficult to even take phone calls - I need visuals when taking in information, I think.

stories.summary: Maura Higgins and her professional dance partner Mark Ballas are through to the next round of Dancing with the Stars on US television. On ABC on Tuesday, the Longford woman  and Ballas danced a Tango to Rihanna's Only Girl (in the World) as part of the show's first-ever Super Bowl Night. They received a standing ovation from members of the audience and 33 points out of a possible 40 from the judges. Guest judge Joe Buck said: "You, Maura, have made me proud to be Irish tonight. You are amazing." Judge Bruno Tonioli described the routine as "thrilling from start to finish" and Higgins as "supremely elegant". "What you two have is this ease of movement. You make it look easy - and it isn't!" he continued.

stories.title: Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh: 'I don't plan to go anywhere'
stories.summary:
For Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh, the death of her younger sister, Bríd, has taken so much. But the memories are still vivid and enriching. Donal O'Donoghue meets her. "The stories I hear and the people I meet through Nationwide are therapeutic," says Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh of how work has helped since her sister, Bríd, died from cervical cancer in January last year, shortly after her 42nd birthday. But grief can catch her still. "I came out of dubbing the other day, happy, and I just started singing 'With your long blonde hair and your eyes blue’ from David Bowie’s ‘Sorrow’ and then I put my hand on the wall and stopped because I thought of Bríd. Sometimes when I feel joy I feel guilt. It was my baby sister; she shouldn’t have died. Hopefully, the next time I’m talking to you that will have passed." Her eyes well. "She was 42 when she died and was 38 when she was diagnosed. For four years she suffered. I watched Bríd on trial drugs. She grabbed at everything to survive. And on the night that she was failing, I just knew. It’s probably the most useless you ever feel, watching someone die because there’s nothing you can do." What helps? "Being with my mother, Áine, is a huge connection to Bríd," she says. "Bríd was her last baby. Jaysus, nobody expected her (Bríd, the youngest of five, was born 10 years after her four siblings) and she wanted for nothing. If she was here now, she’d probably be having a glass of Prosecco. ‘She had notions’ as they might say down the country. "And she had a great relationship with our mother. Like yesterday, I was helping mum with her make-up – she’s 88 but still in great form – and whatever way she looked at me as I put on her eyeliner we both
burst out laughing. That moment with my mother connected me to Bríd. And I love talking about Bríd now.

stories.title: Searches in Waterford after four killed in fire
stories.summary: Gardaí have carried out searches in connection with the investigation into the murders of four members of a family in Co Waterford following an arson attack on their home. Kim English, Philip English and their sons, 12-year-old Callum and nine-year-old Jayden, died after an incendiary device set fire to their home yesterday morning. Two other children, who are aged 14 and six, remain in a critical condition at CHI Crumlin. The incendiary device, believed to have been a petrol bomb, set the house on fire while the family of six were asleep upstairs. The family home in Birchwood Estate remains sealed off for a second day as the forensic examination and evidence gathering continues. Detectives believe the attack is linked to organised crime and drugs related intimidation.

stories.summary: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan has been brought by ambulance to hospital after becoming unwell at an EU Presidency meeting being held at the University of Limerick (UL). An ambulance was called to UL when the minister took ill this afternoon. It is understood that Minister O’Donovan had a seizure at the event in UL. He has previously spoken about having being diagnosed with the neurological condition epilepsy. The minister made reference to the condition when speaking to the media at UL this morning, before attending the event. The minister was hosting a meeting of EU telecommunications ministers which is being held at the UL Sports Arena.

stories.summary: Minister for Culture Patrick O'Donovan has hit out at anonymous briefings from Government and party colleagues, describing them as "hurtful" and "the ultimate betrayal". A newspaper report over the weekend quoted a Fine Gael minister, on condition of anonymity, as saying that "the discussion about whether he [Minister O'Donovan] is well enough to stay in the role is coming for sure". "I do think bringing a person's health into public discourse in the manner in which it was, through an anonymous source, is something that I haven't seen before," he said. "To be honest about it, was quite hurtful, and I have to say that I came out, for want of a better word, with regards to my epilepsy, for a very good reason that I didn't want to have a situation where when I did stutter, that someone would accuse me of, for instance, being drunk." The Limerick County TD has spoken publicly about his recent diagnosis of epilepsy and some of the challenges he has faced in dealing with the condition. "Some days are bad for me, and other days are excruciating in terms of what my life is like," he added.

stories.title: ASML won't be able to meet AI-driven demand in 2027, 2028
stories.summary: ASML said today that AI-driven demand for its chip-printing tools is so strong that it will not be able to fully meet customer demand in 2027 or 2028 and that it is looking at ways to expand capacity as it raised its full-year sales outlook. The world's biggest supplier of chipmaking equipment said customers were already discussing orders after 2027, with some expressing interest in placing orders in 2029 and 2030. The Dutch group forecast sales for the fourth quarter of 2026 of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion, above analyst expectations, with a gross margin of around 57%. That boosted its full-year sales forecast slightly to €44 billion to €45 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected fourth-quarter sales of €14.19 billion at ASML, Europe's largest company by market capitalisation. "A lot of our discussions with our customers now are shifting in fact beyond 2027," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a statement. ASML's customers include TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia, Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, Intel and newcomer Elon Musk and his Terafab, all of whom have expansion plans.

stories.title: Schools closed as French students stage protests
stories.summary: Thousands of protesters marched through central Paris as part of nationwide demonstrations supporting secondary school pupils who have been protesting for better classroom conditions. Swedish activist Greta ⁠Thunberg joined a demonstration outside a secondary school in Paris. With just six months to go before elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, French authorities had been hoping that the protests were easing ahead of half-term holidays starting at the end of this week. But teenagers at schools called lycees - backed by university students, teachers, unions and the far-left opposition party France Unbowed (LFI) - have said their demands have not been met. French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among the crowd of demonstrators in Paris. Outside the Paris city hall, demonstrators - mostly university students - gathered in the afternoon to the tune of an orchestra playing the 'The Rebel Fanfare' from the Star Wars movies.

stories.title: Martinez launches astonishing attack on United hierarchy
stories.summary: Lisandro Martinez has launched an astonishing attack on director of football Jason Wilcox and the Manchester United hierarchy for failing to back under-fire boss Michael Carrick in the summer. Tuesday's 2-0 defeat away to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League extended the Red Devils’ winless run to a fifth match in all competitions and heaped further pressure on the head coach. Pablo Barrios scored after 50 seconds at the Metropolitano, where substitute Ademola Lookman ended a spirited United response by finding the net shortly after Leny Yoro was sent off. But this trip to Spain will not be remembered for the on-field action after Martinez’s unprecedented caustic post-match critique at the way the club has been run. "Really poor (performance), really poor," the fuming Argentina international told Prime Video. "I have to control myself a lot but sometimes it’s a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment.

stories.title: McManus: Leinster SHC reforms can give everyone a chance
stories.summary: Former Antrim hurler Neil McManus has described proposals to revamp the Leinster Hurling Championship as "really positive". Last week, a committee led by former GAA President Nickey Brennan revealed plans to introduce a format including two groups of four teams, with a connection to the Joe McDonagh Cup. It’s understood the proposals will go forward for official endorsement at Congress next year, and, if passed, will be implemented for the 2028 Championship. McManus - who played in three different tiers of championship hurling during his career with the Saffrons - believes the idea will invigorate the Leinster Championship and give greater hope to counties hoping to establish themselves at the top level. "It will read to most people as a two group Leinster Championship, but it’s really three groups and the Joe McDonagh is very much part of the Leinster Championship. "You’ll have to earn your progress, you will get the opportunity from within this structure, even if you’re one of the lowest ranked teams within that 12 to play against the big boys if you can progress in your own group. You’ll earn your chance against the big boys but the chance is there."

stories.title: Carragher avoids bankruptcy after settling tax bill
stories.summary: Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher will not be made bankrupt after settling an unpaid tax bill. Carragher, from Merseyside, spent his entire professional career with Liverpool and was part of the squad who won the Champions League in 2005. He retired in 2013 after making 737 appearances for the club and has since become a pundit with Sky Sports and CBS Sports. A spokesperson for Carragher previously told BBC Sport: "This is a private tax matter that should have been resolved sooner, and the appropriate steps are being taken today to settle it.

stories.title: World Cup-winning coach White takes reins at Fiji
stories.summary: South Africa's 2007 World Cup winning head coach Jake White has been appointed coach of Fiji less than a year out from the next World Cup in Australia. White had been most recently serving as director of rugby with the Bulls, having guided them to three URC Grand Finals in four seasons, losing all three. He parted company with the franchise after the 2024-25 final defeat to Leinster. The South African replaced interim coach Senirusi Seruvakula, who stepped into the role for six months in the wake of Australian Mick Byrne's abrupt departure last April. "I'd like to say we want to have the best-prepared ‌group of players ever to go to ⁠a World Cup. That'll be our challenge," White said. "The theory ‌for me is we want Fiji to play like Fiji but just give them a little bit more structure, a little bit more formation." Fiji performed creditably at the 2023 World Cup, reaching the quarter-finals for the third time in their history after a 22-15 pool stage victory over Eddie Jones's Australian side. They were subsequently beaten 30-24 by England in the quarter-final.

stories.title: Basic Income for the Arts: first recipients to hear this week
stories.summary: The first tranche of successful applications for the new Basic Income for the Arts scheme will be notified this week, the Minister for Culture Patrick O'Donovan has confirmed today. Under the scheme, 2,000 practicing professional artists based in the Republic of Ireland will receive €325 per week for three years. The minister confirmed that up to 750 successful applicants will be notified this week. The process for this scheme has been underway since February 2026, when the Minister announced the successor scheme to the original pilot scheme. The main objective of the Basic Income for the Arts scheme is to support professional artists whose creative practice is based in Ireland. Professional, practicing artists based in the Republic of Ireland were invited to apply for the scheme earlier this year, and just over 10,000 applications were received.

stories.title: What happens when we place too much responsibility on children?
stories.summary: Niamh Delmar is a Chartered Registered Counselling Psychologist, mental health writer, and media contributor. When parents place too much responsibility and are overly dependent on their children, it is referred to as parentificiation. Unhealthy boundaries and unrealistic expectations feature as young people take on adult roles as cleaners, babysitters, supporters or mediators. They are expected to serve the psychological and practical needs of parents. There are two types of parentification: emotional and instrumental. A parent overly shares about relationships, life struggles and their past, or delegates excessive duties. Emeshment and over-involvement can overshadow childhood experiences. While some levels of responsibility in the young years foster life skills and resilience, children need to be cognitively and physiologically ready. Their brains are not fully developed until age 25. Ongoing stress impacts the developing individual neurologically and physiologically. A child who is an emotional crutch to a parent, or a protector from an aggressor, gets stretched beyond their capacity.

stories.title: Increase in industrial greenhouse gas emissions forecast
stories.summary: Ireland's industrial greenhouse gas emissions are projected to rise again in the coming years, with industry and waste now expected to be the second worst-performing sector after transport at meeting its climate targets, according to the Climate Change Advisory Council. The council has warned that the measures currently planned by the Government are not sufficient to deliver the emissions reductions required by 2030. In its latest annual review of the industry and waste sector, it said industrial emissions have fallen for four consecutive years and are now almost 16% below their 2018 levels. However, it warned that this progress is expected to stall, with emissions projected to rise again towards the end of the decade. By 2030, industrial emissions are projected to be just 11.6% below their 2018 levels. This would be substantially short of the Government's target of a 35% reduction.

stories.title: Fresh fears raised over prevalence of nitrous oxide use
stories.summary: Fresh fears have been raised over the prevalence of the use of nitrous oxide in Ireland. Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, is typically inhaled from canisters or balloons to produce a short term high. Its proper use is as pain relief in medicine and dentistry, and as a propellant in catering, particularly for things like whipped cream. Recreational use has increased in recent years, particularly among young people. Inhalation of nitrous oxide often makes users feel light-headed. In certain cases, its use can trigger numbness of the hands and feet, or spinal cord damage, which is referred to as neurotoxicity.

stories.title: Exports to US, EU push China towards record trade surplus
stories.summary: China's exports soared in September, official data showed todayy, putting the country on course for a record annual trade surplus that is likely to increase calls for rebalancing trade from major partners, including the European Union and the US. Exports rose 36.3% year-on-year according to China's customs administration, far exceeding the 25.7% rise predicted by a Bloomberg survey of analysts. Imports also spiked 31% in September, but the world's second-largest economy still recorded a trade surplus of $133.5 billion, the largest monthly figure since January 2025. China's cumulative trade surplus through the end of September reached $938.1 billion, putting it on course to break the record $1.2 trillion surplus it recorded last year. With domestic demand weak by comparison - retail sales grew just 0.4% year-on-year in August - Beijing has relied on exports to meet its annual growth target of 4.5% to 5%. But the boom in shipments has triggered pushback from major markets including the US - which launched a bruising trade war against China last year - and Europe.

stories.title: 11 missing after two ships struck off Bulgaria
stories.summary: Eleven people were reported missing after two merchant ships were struck off the Bulgarian coast in the latest sign of increasing spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned the Russian ambassador after drones struck a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship, while another vessel was also hit and sank further north off the coast of the NATO and EU member. Black Sea shipping has been hit by growing fallout from the Ukraine-Russia war in recent months. Mr Radev said the Ukrainian-owned cargo ship Chelsea 3 was "hit by three aerial drones", and shortly afterwards another ship was "struck" and sank. "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party. However ... logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of the Russian Federation," he wrote, calling the attack "unacceptable". The presidency later identified the sunken ship as the HS Dignity, a Guinea-Bissau flagged cargo vessel and said it went down 17 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian town of Krapets.

stories.title: No need for in-form Lonergan to jump too quickly - Treacy
stories.summary: Tommy Lonergan should not feel compelled to make the jump to pastures new too quickly as the Waterford striker underlined his recent excellence for club and country last week, according to former Republic of Ireland winger Keith Treacy. The 22-year-old scored a brace at Turners Cross last Tuesday as the Ireland under-21s beat a star-studded England 3-1 to book their place in the European Championship play-offs. That was the third U21 match in a row in which he had found the net as Jim Crawford's side revived their qualification campaign. Three days after is heroics in Cork, Lonergan fired in Waterford's second as they stunned Bohemians in the Club Orange Men's FAI Cup semi-final at Dalymount Park. It's been an excellent season for the Meathman, who has scored 14 goals in 30 matches in the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division. In light of that, interest in Lonergan is growing, including from the other side of the Irish Sea where he had a previous spell at Waterford's sister club Fleetwood Town.
